reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Occurs when alcohol is consumed by a patient taking disulfiram, used as a deterrent in alcohol dependence
Symptoms begin within minutes of alcohol ingestion and include flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations and chest tightness
More severe reactions cause marked hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnoea and, rarely, arrhythmias or cardiovascular collapse
The reaction is caused by accumulation of acetaldehyde due to inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase
Similar 'disulfiram-like' reactions can be provoked by metronidazole, certain cephalosporins and other agents
Patients must be counselled to avoid all sources of alcohol including some mouthwashes, tonics and topical or oral preparations
Management is supportive, with fluids and antiemetics; there is no specific antidote and the reaction is self-limiting as acetaldehyde is cleared
The enzyme inhibition is long-lasting, so reactions can occur for up to two weeks after stopping disulfiram
reference.pathophysiology: Ethanol is normally metabolised to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase, and acetaldehyde is then oxidised to acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so when alcohol is consumed, acetaldehyde accumulates to concentrations many times higher than normal. Acetaldehyde is a potent vasoactive and toxic intermediate that causes cutaneous vasodilatation, catecholamine and histamine effects, and stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, producing the flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension of the reaction. Because the enzyme inhibition is irreversible, recovery of aldehyde dehydrogenase activity depends on synthesis of new enzyme, explaining the prolonged period of susceptibility after the drug is stopped.
additionalDifferentials: Acute coronary syndrome (chest pain and diaphoresis)
Carcinoid syndrome or other flushing disorders
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the temporal relationship to alcohol intake
Blood pressure and cardiac monitoring during the reaction
Electrocardiogram to assess for arrhythmia or ischaemia in severe cases
Careful history of hidden alcohol sources and disulfiram-like agents
Blood alcohol concentration where diagnosis is unclear
redFlags: Chest pain or signs of myocardial ischaemia
reference.prognosis: Most reactions are unpleasant but self-limiting, resolving over hours as acetaldehyde is metabolised. Severe reactions with marked hypotension or cardiac effects can occasionally be life-threatening, particularly in patients with cardiovascular disease.
pitfalls: Failing to warn patients about hidden sources of alcohol in mouthwashes, tonics and topical preparations
Not recognising that metronidazole and some cephalosporins cause a similar reaction
Assuming safety immediately after stopping disulfiram despite persisting enzyme inhibition
Mistaking a severe reaction for acute coronary syndrome and overlooking the drug-alcohol interaction
management: Stop further alcohol exposure and manage supportively, as most episodes are self-limiting once acetaldehyde is metabolised
Intravenous fluids and supine positioning for hypotension, with continuous blood pressure and cardiac monitoring
Antiemetics for nausea and vomiting, with supplemental oxygen if the patient is breathless
Vasopressor support and treatment of arrhythmia or cardiovascular collapse in severe reactions, particularly in those with cardiovascular disease
Counsel on strict avoidance of all alcohol sources including some mouthwashes, tonics and topical or oral preparations, and of disulfiram-like agents such as metronidazole and certain cephalosporins
Review the continued role of disulfiram within a structured alcohol-dependence programme
Escalate to critical care if hypotension or cardiac effects prove refractory
